utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. I see that we have some problems with the transcript in e-court. It is looking very strange. If there's nothing to discuss at the outset of today's hearing, the witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Tolimir, we received your request for an extension of time for your cross-examination. I would appreciate if you could be as short as possible, although this is a very important witness for you, of course, but we will not restrict your time, but please focus on the time especially because we have the last day of the hearing this week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet everyone present, and may this hearing be concluded in keeping with God's will and not my own. I will try to conclude during the first hour that had originally been assigned to me, but only if I receive short answers. I have only seven questions left, but I keep receiving very long answers, that is why I asked for an extension just to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Palic. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. He has the floor. Mr. Tolimir. And again, if you need a break at any point in time, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you. Good morning to everyone again. I'd like to greet Ms. Palic and may this be concluded in keeping with God's will. Yesterday you were shown P2192.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see it again in e-court today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Next you were shown another photograph of the 24th of August, which is identical to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the number is, though, of that photograph. I just want to make sure whether -- that there are no differences between the two and to know whether both of them were admitted under the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the meantime, can you tell us this: Was this -- was your house destroyed or was your house the one you marked at P2192? You marked on P2187, actually.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were marking your house yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was your house on the photograph where you marked it or did you mark another house? It is P2187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's now coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see two red indications, one which resembles an arrow, and another one just in front of the wood. Where was your house exactly?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The larger marking?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The walls of the house were still standing, given that it had been a solid building. They stood until 2003, when we went back to Zepa for the first time. The roof was gone, and looking from the side of Boksanica, because that's where the shells came from, the walls were simply pierced through, both the outer wall and the inner walls. They all ended up in the rear of the house. The house was basically riddled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On this photograph of the 27th of July, can we see your house?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the spot where the house had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the other picture next, taken in August, on the 24th of August. It is 2187, which I originally asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, can you tell us whether on this photograph too, from August, we can see your house?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see the walls of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you discussed your husband being told by an UNPROFOR representative that his house would be targeted and that he should move his family.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you on good terms with the UNPROFOR representative and were you on good terms with UNPROFOR in general in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were in good relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about any ABiH attacks on UNPROFOR positions in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such attacks. I don't know of any and I believe there weren't any. Perhaps you can tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at D55, paragraph 22, item 94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to interrupt you for a moment to clarify the correct number of the last photograph we have seen. It is recorded that this was P2187, but I was told it should be 2178. Could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I permutated the figures, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see this photograph which was taken by Mr. Bezruchenko, an OTP investigator who was also in Zepa when you left Zepa. On page 25 of the book, paragraph 94, he describes how on the 20th of July UNPROFOR was attacked by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 94, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It says that: "The defenders of Zepa saw the negotiations between their authorities and the VRS as a sign of inevitable collapse of the enclave." These are the words of Mr. Bezruchenko. "In that situation they no longer cared for co-operation with UNPROFOR and did not need UNPROFOR any longer. In an attempt to seize UNPROFOR's weapons on the 20th of July, the ABiH attacked the compound of the Ukrainian company with heavy machine-gun fire and hand grenades. The second floor of the Ukrainian company building was hit with a heavy weapon which destroyed the first aid station and the medicine stock." And then he goes on. Do you know anything about this attack and do you know why it took place?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What date does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of July? Well, I was in Zepa at the time and I should have known had there been any attacks on UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was targeted by the Serb army from the Serb positions. Mr. Bezruchenko, if I pronounced his name correctly, or whoever it is that wrote the book -- well, co-operation with UNPROFOR in Zepa was a good one. It was a small formation of the Ukrainian battalion. In order to clarify, I want to describe the conduct and behaviour of UNPROFOR representatives in Zepa. The representatives of our authorities had a good relationship with them but only because they had great communication skills, and I include my husband and the representatives of civilian authorities. They gave it their all to have a fruitful co-operation. Mr. Dudnjik was the commander of the UNPROFOR unit in Zepa, and Avdo communicated with him well. This obviously concerns another officer. What I'm trying to say is this: Who were the Ukrainians in Zepa, just by way of an example. When shells started falling on Zepa in March 1995, people complained. Avdo tried to intervene with UNPROFOR so that UNPROFOR would ask the Serb side to stop shelling. It wasn't Dudnjik but some other representatives at the check-point at Portici [phoen], when the residents reported the shells landing, responded by saying, These are our brethren. They did not behave as UN representatives. They behaved as members of a religious group, of a faith. I remember being awoken during the night when I heard shots. It turned out to be Ukrainian soldier firing at the hospital because his brother had been killed in the theatre around Sarajevo. To an extent, I can understand their behaviour, but the Ukrainians always took the side of the Serbs. But the representatives of civilian authorities in Zepa and military authorities in Zepa did their utmost to keep that communication going. There were no attacks on them. And as for this Bezruchenko, he can put anything on paper. Anyone can, but I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since I'm short of time, please bear in mind to keep your answers short. If needed, we'll ask for additional time for you to explain things to the Chamber, but just tell us this for starters: Whether you were in Zepa on the 20th of July or not?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. You've already asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you in Zepa on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 71 of the same book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 75 in e-court -- 71. So that Ms. Palic can see it. We see it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 71, we can see it now in our language as well. It says: "On the 15th of July, major escalation of situation in the enclave was reported as soldiers of the 285th Brigade surrounded and belonged the base and some OPs and presented Ukrainians with an ultimatum to surrender their weapons. Communication with OP 6 and OP 5 was lost. BiH soldiers blocked the roads between the Ukrainian company base, and OP 5 and OP 9 were blocked by wood and rocks. About 100 soldiers also surrounded the compound and radio station and threatened to open fire if weapons were not surrendered." And so on and so forth. My question is: Do you recall this situation? Since Zepa is small, every shot is heard, including anything that was done against UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a silly question. UNPROFOR was 150 metres from my house, the base, and the check-points were at the lines. That's one thing. Another thing, I don't recall any great misunderstandings between UNPROFOR and the representatives of authorities in Zepa. We did seek UNPROFOR's protection because we were a UN-protected area. We sought protection from the Serb forces. Objectively they couldn't provide it. That is why we requested help from the UN in Sarajevo. Nothing occurred, and it was only logical that weapons were then sought and the men were sent to the lines. What were we supposed to do? For you to wait to enter Zepa like you did Srebrenica, for all of us to be killed? No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 72 next. "The next few days the battle for Zepa was picking up. The situation of the 285th Brigade was becoming progressively desperate, and Colonel Palic decided to disarm the Ukrainian company of UNPROFOR. On the 16th of July, Palic reported: "'They are attacking us more and more strongly. They have strong artillery support as well as manpower and they are pushing further, mostly from the direction of Han Pijesak. We are doing whatever we can. We will be holding out. People are quite exhausted. The territory that we are defending is too big for our unit. I cannot tell you now for how long I will be able to hold out. We are disarming UNPROFOR in accordance with the previously given instructions.'" This probably describes the grave situation you were in. Did you receive instructions from Sarajevo that UNPROFOR should be disarmed and Palic, I believe, worked according to those instructions and not of his own will?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 73. Let's see what was taken away. This report is consistent with the UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo report dated the 16th of July, 1995. According to the report, BiH army soldiers surrounded three Ukrainian OPs and threatened the OPs' personnel, capturing their weapons and ammunition. "At 1100 hours, the VRS launched an infantry attack supported by tanks and artillery between OP 1 and OP 8. At 1656, the ABiH surrounded OP 5 personnel, demanding their arms and equipment. By the close of the day, the VRS reached OP 2 at Boksanica and threatened to kill the Ukrainian soldiers in case of NATO air presence over their positions. The Ukrainian company also reported that heavy artillery, mortar and tank fire around the enclave persisted. The Ukrainian company UNPROFOR presence was now restricted to the Ukrainian base in OPs 3, 5, and 7, meaning that all the others were seized. ABiH soldiers surrounded OP 5 demanding weapons of the OP personnel." I won't read any further, but in paragraph 74 we can see what equipment was seized and from what OPs. Do you know anything about the blockade of UNPROFOR and weapons being taken away from them at their observation post?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was blocked, together with the Zepa population, by the Serb army. That's one thing. And apart from that, I don't know what you are trying to say by everything that you read out. I don't know that UNPROFOR was maltreated by us in Zepa. If they had, they would certainly have reported that. And I don't believe that UNPROFOR had any bad experience with the BiH authorities in Zepa. And apart from that, what you have read out only shows the atrocious conditions that we lived in. And Avdo did not take the weapons that were given to the Ukrainian battalion. They were supposed to defend us. But what did you expect us to do? To let you tie our hands and kill us off. Of course we defended ourselves, but never did we take action against either the Ukrainians or the Serb civilians. And, well, the soldiers are something else, of course. Soldiers get killed. That's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. We saw a minute ago that Avdo Palic says that he is disarming UNPROFOR according to instructions. I want to ask you the following. If you look at D53. Can we please see it? Whether Avdo Palic received instructions to attack both UNPROFOR and the VRS. Instructions from Sarajevo. Let us take a look at this document and then you'll see that it wasn't just the will of Avdo Palic but an order by the central authorities and the Main Staff. I'm not attacking your husband. Let's see what it says. D53, you see it reads: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army General Staff. 17 June. Preparations for offensive combat operations. Order. Person to verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH Army, Army General Rasim Delic. And on the occasion of the great success achieved by the units of the BH Army and the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde, as well as on the basis of intelligence that the aggressive forces command of the protection regiment in Han Pijesak," and so on, "I hereby issue the following order: "1: Execute all preparations in the command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations." Offensive operations means attacks. "Item 2: Plan realistic tasks which will assure certain success. "Item 3: The General Staff of the BH Army will regulate by an order the commencement of offensive combat activities." Here is my question to you: Did your husband complain that he was being pressurised from Sarajevo that they should take military action from Zepa against the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo was a very rational man and I'm sure that nobody could order him to commit a crime. What you are showing me here, well, it would have been much better for you if you had saved Avdo's life. I suppose that you should have asked him that and you probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. If I had his statement, if I had asked him, I would show it to you now.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you made a big mistake, you see. You should have kept him alive. He would have been much more useful to you alive than dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please take a look at D92. Since you are asking me, I must show you a document about that. D92. The 23rd of August, when your husband was in detention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a criminal report. Let us go to page 3, please. This criminal report was drafted on 23 August 1995, and we see the names of some persons, 149 in all. Let's go to the last but one page. The statement of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should indicate that this is a criminal report of the VRS to avoid misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's a criminal report drafted on the 23rd of August and it most probably contains information about Avdo Palic, because Ms. Palic wanted me to show something that he said. It wasn't my original intention to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us see. The statement of reasons says: "During the preliminary criminal investigation, the authorised personnel undertook a series of operative activities aimed at documenting the crimes set forth in the disposition of this criminal report."

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but what does the disposition say? What were they accused of? I have no idea what this is all about. Obviously you submitted a criminal report against any man in Zepa who was able bodied. This is one of the lists and you can find as many lists of this kind on the internet as you want. Every able-bodied man was indicted by the Serb machinery, indicted for crimes. But where are the crimes committed by the Zepa army, by the troops in Zepa? And you think that the fact that we defended ourselves justifies your attacks. That six brigades were attacking such a small place. I know that you cannot answer this, but I cannot but ask you this: Six brigades are attacking such a small place and you are -- and here you are mentioning some names. I was able to see some names. I guarantee that none of them ever committed a crime. Defending your life, your family, your home, your town cannot be considered a crime. None of them went to attack Banja Luka or wherever you are from. But you came from the other end of Bosnia-Herzegovina to attack us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, I have to interrupt you and to tell you it is the right of the accused to put questions to you. This is the way such a trial is going on. It is -- I understand very well that this is a very difficult situation for you and that you are quite emotional. I understand that. On the other hand, we want to hear from you your knowledge about facts, and it is not up to you to qualify the kind of questions Mr. Tolimir is putting to you. It is the Chamber to control -- to have control over the way the accused is putting questions to you. And please wait until you receive a question before you start answering. I hope that helps to calm down the situation a bit. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to read the statement of reasons for Ms. Palic to see that this information was obtained through interviewing eye-witnesses. I will now show why this was all done. Could we please scroll down so we can see -- or, rather, scroll up to see the second paragraph in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says under 2: "On 4 June 1992, at a place called Riza, near Brloznik village, at the Han Pijesak-Godjenje-Stoborani cross-roads, they carried out an attack on a column of military vehicles and soldiers of the VRS. On which occasion they killed 43 VRS soldiers and officers, took 30 soldiers prisoner, burned and destroyed a large number of vehicles and other materiel and technical equipment, perfidiously liquidated injured soldiers from the attacked column at the scene of the incident in contravention of the rules of international law." This is why this criminal report was filed against these 149 persons on the list. I don't want to remind you anymore but I'm just telling you that this is -- was done because of the event on 4 June 1992. Do you know anything about that event? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fail to understand why you are asking such questions. I would never do that if I were you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, it was a very simple question, do you know anything about that event. If you know, please tell us, if you don't know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, sir, this was one of the first offensives against Zepa. I do apologise, but this man is wearing me out. This was one of the first Serb -- or it would be more rightly called Chetnik offensive against Zepa because they took pride in being Chetniks at the time. A column of Serb soldiers set out from Pale in 40 vehicles under the pretext of transporting food to the troops on the Zepa mountain. There was a small facility where there was a small air force unit, five or six soldiers. I have their exact strength in one of my registers. They set off in 40 vehicles, and there was a tank at the head of the convoy, under the pretext of transporting food. Actually, it was an attempt by the Serb army to reach Ozlovrh on the Zepa mountain. If that convoy had made it to Mount Zepa then, on the -- we would have been slaughtered on the 4th of June. The same way that people were killed in Visegrad, Foca and other places. But the people of Zepa saw through their pretext. Why should they need 40 vehicles to do what they allegedly wanted to do? And, yes, there were troops at this place and they used all possible means. We didn't even have weapons at the time. This convoy of the JNA, or rather, the Serb army did not arm us. It's a fact that the Serb soldiers killed each other because they were afraid of being taken prisoner, because for ideological reasons or being ideologically indoctrinated they were scared of being taken prisoner, but whoever was killed their bodies were surrendered. There is no one body that was left behind in the area of Zepa that wasn't handed over to the Serb side. There was no one Serb soldier taken prisoner who was not returned and not one of them was mistreated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Since, as you say, the people attacked the convoy to arm themselves, do you know whether your husband allowed that convoy to go -- to move in the direction of Ozlovrh?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were no troops in Zepa. The Zepa Brigade was only established in September. The attack on 4th of June was the moment when the men started to consolidate and create a kernel of troops for Defence. This defence was sporadic. Only those people went there who were brave enough to attack that convoy. They threw rocks, stones, logs, and whatever they had. Avdo wasn't a commander then, nor were there any troops at the time, so he wasn't in a position to allow anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Do you know whether at the time there were orders from Sarajevo to create as many excesses [as interpreted] as possible to make impossible the further co-existence of Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said how the hostilities began in Sarajevo once a person was killed. Do you know what it was about exactly?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Zepa at the time. On the 4th of April there was the first victim. We heard on the news that a police officer was killed and then some persons were killed in a demonstration, two persons, and so there were news about people being killed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they truthful news, do you know who was really killed on the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there, but if all of Bosnia-Herzegovina believes one thing and if their families know that Olga Sucic and Suada Dilberovic were killed and other victims, why shouldn't I believe that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the killing of the soldiers in a convoy -- a JNA convoy leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me about things that I didn't witness in Sarajevo, but I do know that Bosnia-Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state should have been free from the JNA. And when I was leaving Sarajevo on 29 March, I was leaving for Zepa. I travelled four hours from Sarajevo to Rogatica, and under normal circumstances, it would be a little less than an hour -- a little more than an hour, because a convoy of military vehicles was actually entering Sarajevo which means that you were preparing to take Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. I question the relevance of this line of questioning. I've let it go for several questions, but asking every witness who comes here their knowledge about the origins of the war without any direct link to the obvious matters within the knowledge of the witness seems to be a waste of time and doesn't advance any line of defence I can imagine. It seems to be somewhat provocative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness said, "You should have asked Avdo Palic." I simply wanted to show her the information gathered through the interviews, the information about an event that was carried out with the intention to prevent the co-existence between Muslims and Serbs. That's why we read out this criminal report. It's not a small thing to kill 40 and wound 30 soldiers in a column. There are other documents about this and that's why I started asking my questions. Yesterday during examination-in-chief, events in Sarajevo were mentioned. It was the witness herself who said how the war actually began, and that's why I'm now asking the witness about the things that she knows about. I'm not asking anything that she doesn't know about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I don't share your view. You were asking the witness about the truthfulness of media reports. How can she state if that is truthful or not, if these news are reliable or the not? She clearly indicated that at that time she was in Zepa and not in Sarajevo. It is not the purpose of your cross-examination to show her the information gathered through the interviews. You should ask her about her knowledge and not to enter into a debate about your knowledge and her knowledge and what you gathered, what kind of information you gathered about Avdo Palic. This is not the purpose of the cross-examination. Put questions to get information from her she can testify about. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked her whether she knew anything about the killing of the 40 soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss this matter any further with you. Please put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is very important thing in relation to the beginning of the conflict in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry, you may ask her about her knowledge and nothing else. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that soldiers used to come from Srebrenica in large numbers and then together with the military in Zepa they went to carry out attacks against the Main Staff and the VRS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was that Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look at D145. I would like to show the witness the topics that I want to ask about. D145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I would like to put a question to Ms. Palic. Do you know anything about attacks from Srebrenica against the Main Staff and the VRS? This was the core of the question of Mr. Tolimir. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When and where was that Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, do you know anything? If you don't know, just tell it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I'm going to read out the first paragraph of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "On the 23rd of June, 1995, at 0200 hours, a unit of approximately 300 soldiers headed out from Srebrenica, led by Ibrahim Mandzic, the commander of the 280th Brigade, Eastern Bosnia Light Brigade; Vejiz Sabic, the commander of the 284th Light Brigade; his deputy, Semso Salihovic; and a guide, a man called Zoran Cardakovic, a Muslim. The unit's task was to insert itself that same day at approximately 2000 hours into the general sector of Ruzina Voda, Han Pijesak municipality, via Zepa and Radava. This group is equipped with automatic weapons, with a couple of 60-millimetre mortars and some RPGs, rocket propelled grenade." So, take a look at this once again to acquaint yourself with the contents if necessary. It says here that they are going through Zepa into the general sector of Ruzina Voda and Han Pijesak, and that's where the Main Staff was. We saw that in the report that we looked at yesterday that mentioned nine sabotage groups, and that's a report signed by Avdo Palic. My question is: Are you aware of this event of the 23rd of June, when a unit comprising 300 soldiers, together with the soldiers from Zepa Brigade, went to carry out one of the tasks that we read about yesterday? Your husband reported about certain number of casualties and his commander said that 60 Chetniks in total were killed.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. Tell us the following: Is it justified to bring soldiers into the demilitarised zone and then attack from the demilitarised zone the very side which accorded the status of demilitarised zone to that place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mrs. Palic is not a member of an army. How can you ask her about the -- if something is justified, if a military attack is justified? You should ask her questions she can answer. Please move to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to move on to my next question. Can we have P21. Thank you. I would like to see D21, and I have to say what D21 is. It's the agreement about the ceasefire with territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed between Ratko Mladic and Sefer Halilovic on the 8th of May, 1993. So the agreement was signed by Ratko Mladic and Sefer Halilovic and the representatives of UNPROFOR, Philippe Morillon. Can we take a look at the second page that mentions demilitarisation. Article 3, that's what I want to see. Can we have the next page in both languages. You can see Article 3 here: "Every military or paramilitary unit will have either to withdraw from the demilitarised zone or submit/hand over their weapons. Ammunition, mines, explosives and combat supplies in the demilitarized zones will be handed over/submitted to UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know the reason why not all the weapons were handed over to UNPROFOR, and how could it happen that later on there were still some armed soldiers in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the answer to this question. I could answer by posing another question, but this is really pointless and it wears me out. What do you mean? If we were a demilitarised zone from the March -- in March 1995, how come then did the Serbian forces were shelling Zepa if we were a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic. Yesterday you spoke at length about the events up to this agreement. You spoke about refugees, about shelling, and about other things. My question is: Was this agreement signed because both sides committed similar misdeeds, expelled the population, massacred them, and shelled them, and that's the reason why the agreement was signed, do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What agreement are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm talking about the agreement about the demilitarisation. Was that the reason for the demilitarisation, in order to prevent similar attacks and further loss of life?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrival of the UN in Zepa and the demilitarisation was caused exclusively by the sufferings of people in Zepa. That is what I claim. Maybe we could see some evidence and I mean here relevant evidence and not the evidence generated by the Serbian machinery. There were no crimes carried out from Zepa. The army in Zepa carried out no crimes. From 1992 until May 1993, Serbian army attacked Zepa on a continuous basis, by tanks, by infantry and by aeroplanes. In addition to that, the population was starved out. It was a humanitarian catastrophe that went on for months. There were no medicines. The surrounding terrain was mined. There was a large number of people who stepped on a mine and who lost their limbs and they had to be treated in a very difficult situation because there was not enough medicine. And that was the reason why we continuously sent appeals to Sarajevo, to the Sarajevo authorities, to the UNHCR and to the UN. We wanted them to help the people who managed to resist the attacks of the Serbian army. This is a generally known thing, why the enclaves were demilitarised and protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please take a look at the statement of a Prosecution witness dated 11th of April, page 2542, line 23. And 12543, line 16. This was also a Prosecution witness, just like you, and this was the witness who explained what happened to the Serbs who were in the zone that was subsequently demilitarised. So I will read it out to you: "Everything else in my territory, from Skelani onwards, they attacked, they destroyed and they burned down. There were casualties there. Further on, Ratkovici, Fakovici, Stamatovici, Ducici. There's no need for me to list everything, all the villages in the zone of Srebrenica were attacked, except the two villages that I mentioned earlier, within the four kilometres from the centre of the town and along the Drina River. All other villages were attacked and burned down. In each of those villages there were military and civilian casualties." Now, do you know that all Serbian villages around Srebrenica, except two villages in Bratunac, were attacked, destroyed, burned down and their population was expelled?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now asking me about Srebrenica and I don't know about Srebrenica. That's why I rather wouldn't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the Zepa Brigade within the 28th Division that was headquartered in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it yesterday, the Zepa Brigade was the East Bosnia Light Infantry Brigade and I was not aware whether it was in some sort of a larger structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us see what the same witness said at 12680, lines 6 to 14, on the 12th of April: "I think you did not understand my answer given to the Presiding Judge. I mentioned the attack on Kravica. I didn't especially mention the attack on Kravica. All those present in the courtroom should know that the attack on the 7th of January was the most well-known attack, and I was simply talking about the attack on villages such as Kravica. In 1992, there were about 30 similar attacks. So I did not speak specifically about the attack on Kravica on the 7th of January, 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all this seems to be remaining on the subjects of Srebrenica which the witness has indicated is likely outside her knowledge. And secondly, if it's not a protected witness, it may help to inform the witness to provide the name or at least the position of the witness who is giving this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful for the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. That was Momir Nikolic, a Prosecution witness. He testified on the 11th and the 12th of April this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know, Ms. Palic, anything about this event, Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know the details. If I attempted to say anything about this, it would only amount to an improvisation and this is certainly not a place to improvise. I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are right. If you don't have specific knowledge, then tell us. It is not helpful for anybody to receive speculation or hearsay evidence. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mrs. Palic, you remember that in relation to this period you showed a letter dated 28th of November, 1993, on page 62, line 3 onwards. It was your letter, and then we also heard five paragraphs of letters sent by Rajko Kusic to your husband. What I want to know is after that, on the 18th of January, 1993, was this agreement on demilitarisation of Zepa and Srebrenica signed?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. There were such letters between -- before and after demilitarisation. When you talk about the correspondence between my husband and Kusic, they corresponded both before and after that date. That was a letter that Avdo sent via Lari [phoen] and that was before the territory of Zepa was protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Palic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please clarify what you mean by "it was your letter," and what do you mean by page 62, line 3? Are you referring to the transcript of yesterday? We would like to have it clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At page 62, lines 3 onwards, some letters were read out that Ms. Palic provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I want to know if you are referring to the transcript of yesterday or to another document. This is my first request. The second is, what do you mean by "your letter," do you really mean a letter of Ms. Palic, or what do you mean? You should be very clear in your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll give you a direct answer. It was during examination-in-chief when Ms. Palic was asked by Mr. Elderkin at page 62 at line 3 about some of the contents of her husband's letter. Secondly, I had in mind the letter she handed over to the Prosecution. It was stressed that it was she who provided those letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is at least unclear if you say "your letter," that in my understanding, it's a letter of the witness. But now put a question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't mean that she wrote the letter. I believe I mentioned correspondence between her husband and Rajko Kusic. I apologise if it was misinterpreted or if I confused the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Ms. Palic, did you know whether after the signing of the demilitarisation agreement of Zepa and Srebrenica, life there became better? Was food supply improved and other conditions as well?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the situation was stabilised. Humanitarian assistance came more regularly. In terms of biological survival, things did get easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did it continue until July 1995 when the well-known events occurred that you testified to?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I already said that the situation worsened as early as March 1995. That's when Serb provocations became regular and that the peace was gone. It was in early March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So as not to have to go back to the document, but I read out yesterday how it was ordered from Sarajevo that attacks should be carried out from the zones. Was this in breach of the agreement as well as against the improved conditions that you lived in as you described?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know -- wouldn't have an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know of any preparations carried out by the army and the brigades in Zepa and Srebrenica to continue waging war by arming themselves and carrying out sabotage activities?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at D65 so that the witness could see. It is D67 actually. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It describes how Zepa was being armed by air, by helicopters, and I will put my question after I have read out the introductory part. This document was drafted by the intelligence administration in Sarajevo on the 13th of July, 1995, after Srebrenica had fallen. It was sent to Alija Izetbegovic via the 1st Corps commander. This document was sent by Army General Rasim Delic, at least his name appears in the signature block. In the first paragraph he states: "In view of the situation of our enclaves during the preceding period, the Army General Staff has undertaken a series of military activities and procedures to organise the members of the army and the enclaves and prepare them for possible developments, primarily defence of the existing free territory and planned engagement and preparations for future joint operations and planned operations. Specifically, the following has been done for Srebrenica and Zepa." Bullet point 1: "To start with, lethal assets and materiel and technical equipment were brought in on foot in fairly small quantities." The second bullet point: "Seventeen helicopter sorties were carried out, in each of which the helicopter was hit." The third bullet point: "In this way we transported a number of seriously wounded and residents of Srebrenica." My question is this: Did you know there was an air-lift operation in existence between Zepa and ABiH territory in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when UNPROFOR arrived in Zepa in 1993 and up until perhaps March 1995, from time to time we did have helicopter evacuation. Especially in 1993 there were several such evacuations of the wounded and sick. A small number of people were also taken out as part of family reunification. All those helicopter sorties were agreed on with the Serb side through UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. How come, then, such quantities of weapons and ammunition was transported on board such helicopters as Mr. Delic specified in this document?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I needn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, why were those helicopters shot down if it was agreed upon with the Serb side and why was this kept secret from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's up to the VRS to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the following pages of the document. I believe there is a table on the next page. Here you can see what weapons arrived, and let's go to the next page. We can see here the totals of what arrived in Zepa and in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we see the last page so that we can see Rasim Delic, army general, signed the document. Thank you. Could we next have 1D32, which states that the Serb side did not provide authorisation for such flights and that the position of the VRS was that the flights would be used to transport weapons and ammunition. Could we please have 1D23 -- or 1D32. It's a document of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Army General Staff of the 17th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The third paragraph begins with the word "the aggressor." The 7th line from the top. "On the 16th of February, 1995, the aggressor filed a request with UNPROFOR to declare Zepa a non-demilitarised zone with the following rationale: BH Army helicopter flights supplying weapons and ammunition have been registered; movements of the BH Army have been registered in the Zepa sector; accusing members of the Ukrainian Battalion that they are covering up for the activities and intentions of the BH army; on the night between 15 and 16th February 1995, our helicopters were seen flying over and that infantry fire was opened." The document was signed by Enver Hadzihasanovic, Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let's have a look at the order itself and then I'll have a question. Item one of the order, OG units to be put at full combat readiness. Second item, OG units deployed in Srebrenica to be on stand-by for co-ordinated action with the 1st Zepa Light Brigade. So it's a coordination between Zepa and Srebrenica. Item 3, bringing units to full combat readiness and other measures must be taken under strict secrecy in order to eliminate any grounds on the aggressor's part for violations of the agreement on the demilitarised zone. Item 4, until the helicopter is evacuated, take full measures of camouflaging it as well as security measures as ordered. Item 5, should the helicopter be found in your contacts with UNPROFOR representatives, take the position that its purpose was to transport political representatives of Srebrenica/Zepa. Does this indicate as to whether the VRS approved such flights or were they illegal? Can you see that from the order signed by Enver Hadzihasanovic, Chief of Staff of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not comment what someone else wrote. I only know that the flights from Zepa to Tuzla and Sarajevo were in -- carried out in agreement with Serb representatives through UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, did you hear that one of the helicopters crashed and that there were some 12 casualties?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did shoot down a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, you say "you did shoot down." I think you are referring to the Army of the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I mean the VRS. I apologise for being somewhat confusing because I'm being confused. Yes, the Serb army fired at the helicopter, bringing it down. There were a number of casualties. Many people died and those who survived were seriously injured. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please again have D55. Paragraph 17 at page 6 in the Serbian language, which is probably the same in the English version. Paragraph 17, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both versions are in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have for the witness a version in a language she understands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 17. "UNPROFOR's request for a fact-finding mission was rejected by Colonel Palic, further straining relations between UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo and the command of the 285th Brigade." Did you know why UNPROFOR was not allowed to approach the helicopters to carry out an inspection in order to ascertain why they were shot down and how the people died?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any details, but this seems to be the same author, this Bezruchenko person. It is a fact that this agreement mediated by UNPROFOR was not honoured. Not once did you try to conclude an agreement and then open fire or arrest the negotiators [as interpreted]. Avdo was hurt emotionally by this incident and he never took human casualties lightly. He was well shaken because so many lives were lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Palic. Mr. Bezruchenko is an OTP investigator. He studied all the documents, both the VRS and ABiH documents. At page 11 of this document, in paragraph 35, he wrote the following. This is paragraph 35, I believe. He says precisely what you did: "On the 15th of June, 1995, the army of BiH launched massive offensive operations to live the siege of Sarajevo." He also states that, in the fourth line, Ramiz Becirovic sent an order on the 20th of June, 1995, to all the brigades of the 28th Division to launch sabotage actions. In item 36 he states: "The 285th Brigade began implementing the order with immediate effect. According to Colonel Palic's report, between the 20th and 28th of June, 1995, nine sabotage and reconnaissance groups from Zepa went in the rear of the VRS. These groups killed about 40 VRS soldiers and wounded dozens ..." And so on and so forth. Do you know anything about these military activities ordered from Sarajevo to be undertaken from the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer this question I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir, you said: "He says precisely what you did," end of quote. I think you are not referring to Ms. Palic, but to the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I keep having this feeling that I'm being be misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It could be verified with the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Palic, are you able to answer this question, do you know anything about the military activities ordered from Sarajevo to be undertaken from the demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I said a number of times that I don't know and I keep receiving this question time and again in different shapes. I don't know about this. My husband was a very sensible man and he would never have come to terms with the commission of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. If you don't know, just tell us that you don't know. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't even think your husband would do this of his own accord. We had a witness here who said that the population objected to attacks being carried out from Zepa against the VRS, stating that this could worsen and tighten their relations. I just wanted to know whether you were familiar with such rumours and such positions stated?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness answered this question. Please carry on to the next question. And bear in mind the time you are spending.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I have run out of time, then I have no further questions because I want to finish within the time allotted. I thank Ms. Palic for all the answers she gave and I apologise to her if I had to ask some questions not because of her but to defend myself because I've been accused of something I haven't done. I wish her a safe journey and a safe return to her home and family, and may God bless her and protect her. Thank you, Ms. Palic. Have a good trip and God bless you. Mr. President, I have concluded my cross-examination and the Defence has no more questions for this witness. Thank you, Mr. President, for the assistance you provided us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. However, I would like to stress that I didn't stop you. I just said, "and bear in mind the time you are spending." I didn't stop you. I just want to put it on the record. If you don't have any more questions in your cross-examination, then Mr. Elderkin has the floor for his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I may just have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Re-examination will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Palic.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up on questions that you were asked both yesterday at the transcript page 13331, and the question involved who, in fact, interrogated your husband after his capture by the Bosnian Serb army. And you were asked the question: "Q. Thank you, Ms. Palic, I want to ask you to be precise. A moment ago you said that nobody saw your husband except me, and you should have said when I saw him. You also said that I interrogated him in an apartment. Can you tell us who said that and when?" The question continues. Again this morning you were asked at page 11, lines 2 to 3, in the context of who interrogated your husband: "If I had his statement, if I had asked him ..." Then the question again continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So in the context of that cross-examination, I'd ask, please, to see Exhibit P487.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I haven't shown you this document before so I'd like you to take a moment, please, to read through it. The origin, the date at the top, the content, and who wrote it, please.

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the document but I had the information. The handicap in my struggle is that I don't have access to such documents, but I do have information that -- and I'll ask the Presiding Judge to give me permission to do so at the end. My husband was actually trapped by Zdravko Tolimir. Zdravko Tolimir was the representative of the Serb side, Avdo Palic was the representative of the Bosniak side. If Zdravko Tolimir would have been taken prisoner, Avdo Palic would have been responsibile. The way it happened, it's the other way around. It's a fact, though, that there are statements that the soldiers who took my husband prisoner handed him over to officers Furtula and Tolimir. In one statement it is said that it was at the source of the Zepa. In other statements there is no such precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just because we can't see on the English translation the source of the document, I'd ask first of all that we could see the second page of the English translation, but I just want to read out on that first page the document was dated 28th of July of 1995 and it's sent to recipients the VRS Main Staff Sector for Intelligence and Security, General Krstic personally, and the Drina Corps Intelligence and Security organ. It's sent from the command of the Rogatica Brigade, and the title is "Mine Disposition in Zepa." And it starts: "During the conversation with Avdo Palic, we found out that the minefields and individual mines were laid at the following locations."

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now I've put that in context, if we could see the rest of the English translation, there should be a second page which has the footer of the document, and we can see that the typed signature block is "Major General Zdravko Polimir." Now, within that context excuse myself for interrupting and ask you to continue whether you have any knowledge, or based on your review of this document, whether it's your understanding that General Tolimir was involved in the questioning of your husband after his capture?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I have, General Tolimir was involved in the talks and he was the one with whom Avdo co-operated. To my knowledge, when Avdo was kidnapped from the UN base on the 27th of July in the morning when he was invited to the talks, he was kidnapped from the base and the soldiers handed him over to Furtula and Tolimir, which means that Tolimir was present when the prisoner was brought in. Logically, Tolimir knew about his arrest and possibly ordered it. Then there's information that Avdo was held in Zoran Carkic's apartment in Rogatica for 15 days which fits in because there are witnesses who said that Avdo was taken to the secret prison in Bijeljina on the 15th of August, and I have information from the Ukrainian soldier that Avdo during the first 15 days was at Rogatica and he was being questioned. There's information that -- or, rather, there are testimonies that he was questioned by the officers of the Main Staff of the VRS. This gentleman was one of the most important men in the Main Staff, which means one of those who conducted the deportation of the Zepa population. Secondly, Beara was appointed, but without this man, Tolimir, nothing could happen in Zepa and nothing concerning Avdo happened without Tolimir knowing. This -- I state that with full responsibility and this is proof of that too. I'm in the position to document some things but not others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, thank you very much. I don't have any more questions in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we see the first page of the English version again, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you an additional question, Ms. Palic. You just said that your husband was kidnapped from the UN base on the 27th of July and then was handed over to Furtula and Mr. Tolimir. What is the source of your knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source is the witness statement -- or, rather, the statement of the soldiers who arrested or kidnapped my husband and handed him over. An investigation was conducted by a commission of the VRS and a number of persons were interviewed, among them the soldiers who kidnapped him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you mentioned Mr. Carkic and that Avdo Palic was taken to his apartment. What is the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: ESMA PALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also the statement of Zoran Carkic that he gave to the investigators of that commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Palic, this concludes the questioning for you in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague to provide you -- to provide us with your knowledge and we are very glad that you were able to stand this very difficult and emotionally difficult situation. Now you are free to return to your normal life, and the Chamber would like to thank you again. We will adjourn now for the first break and resume at 11.00 with the next witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome, Ms. Hasan. Good to see you again in the courtroom. Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honour. The next witness is ready and may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And help me, which protective measures are in place for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: He will be testifying under a pseudonym and with face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness should be brought in, please. We go into closed session to enable him to get into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please wait a moment, we have to arrange something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, again, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan for the Prosecution is now putting questions to you during the examination-in-chief. Ms. Hasan, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, before I begin, the last time this witness testified he received a caution and it may be appropriate to give him that same caution this time around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, we have in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence a rule which I would like to read out to you as a caution. I quote, this is Rule 90(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand what I have read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 7336 displayed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, without reading anything aloud, could you please look at the screen and confirm whether the name that appears under pseudonym PW-064 is your name?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I offer the pseudonym sheet into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, have you recently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7336 shall be assigned Exhibit P2193, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number. It is not properly recorded, at least in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 7336 shall be assigned Exhibit P2193, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see it was recorded correctly in LiveNote. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, have you recently had the opportunity to listen to your testimony from the Popovic case, which you gave on the 23rd, 26th and 27th of March, 2007?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did you listen to that testimony in your own language?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was the evidence that you gave in that trial true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I would then offer Mr. President, the transcript of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's a problem with the microphone. Try it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So given that it looks like it was recorded, the answer of the witness was recorded, I would then offer the transcript of this witness's testimony from the Popovic case, namely 65 ter 6517 and 6518, into evidence, which have already provisionally been given exhibit numbers P1030 and 1031, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received, the first one under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And at this stage I'd also offer into evidence all the associated exhibits admitted through the witness in that trial, namely 65 ter 6519 through to 6529, in addition to 65 ter 1327, 992, and 3377. Again all of these exhibits have been provisionally given exhibit numbers P1032 through 1045. And just one other clarification, it seems that 65 ter 1327 that I've just referred to as an associate exhibit, has already been admitted as P1042 in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Do all documents have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm told that they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the first six documents are under seal and also P1043 under seal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received. P1032, 1033, 1034, 1035, 1036, 1037, and 1043, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And with your leave, Mr. President, I will now read a summary of the witness's prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If I may, just for the first bit, go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In the evening on the day before the witness saw an execution in Kravica, he recalled being in Bratunac at the municipal building with Srbislav Davidovic, the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Bratunac. While there, he saw buses full of men and civilian policemen at the entrance of the municipal building. The men on the buses asked for water, which the witness provided. The day after seeing the buses carrying the men, the witness went to Konjevic Polje. On his way there, he saw buses carrying women, children, and the elderly moving in the same direction, that is, from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje. En route, he drove through Kravica, and as he passed the farmers' co-operative building, which is what we are referring to as the Kravica warehouse, he saw a man in a green camouflage uniform order five men to lie on their stomachs and then proceed to shoot each of them in the back. The witness also saw a pile of approximately 40 to 50 bodies to the right of where this execution took place. There were between 10 and 20 men in camouflage uniforms walking around in the area that this witness saw. That same evening the witness met with Ljubisa Borovcanin, the deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade, Miroslav Deronjic, the president of the SDS Bratunac, and Srbislav Davidovic, the president of the Executive Board, and maybe some others at the Jasen restaurant in Bratunac. A young man with bandaged hands joined them later at the restaurant. The witness was told during this gathering that a member of the Special Police Unit had been killed and that the young man who had joined them later on had burned his hands after seizing a rifle from a Muslim man. The witness told the group about the killings that he had witnessed previously that day at the Kravica warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am very sorry, we have to check ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We had to check if there is something on the record we have to redact and we will do that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: After seeing Borovcanin, the witness returned to his office, and while in his office that night, he received a call from the municipality instructing him to report to the SDS premises where Colonel Beara was awaiting him. The witness knew that Colonel Beara was a senior officer of the VRS. Colonel Beara inquired about the machinery and manpower the public utility company had at its disposal. The witness told Colonel Beara that the company had two FAP trucks, a small SKIP excavator and men, which had been mobilised to work for the company. Colonel Beara told the witness to prepare the equipment because "there will be a lot of dead and they need to be buried." After some further discussion, Colonel Beara dismissed the witness and told him to await further orders. During the early morning hours, the witness received a call summoning him once again to the SDS premises. Colonel Beara told the witness that a military policeman would accompany him to show him where the location was where they were to dig out graves. The witness left with the military policeman in a military police vehicle to Glogova and was shown where the graves were to be dug out. In the morning, the men mobilised to work for the RAD company were taken by truck --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is there any problem with translation or recording?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I extend my greetings to Ms. Hasan. Could I please hear on which day he received the phone call and on which day he was contacted by Beara because that's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is not an appropriate interruption. Ms. Hasan is reading a summary and she shouldn't be interrupted by that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In the morning, the men mobilised to work for the RAD company were taken by truck to the grave-site location. They attempted to dig the graves using a ULT loader excavator owned by the brickworks Bratunac company, but could not do so. The witness informed Colonel Beara of the problem and was told that a backhoe excavator from the Zvornik Brigade would be sent for them to use. A backhoe excavator arrived in the afternoon from the direction of Kravica or Konjevic Polje, which was then used to dig four graves. The work was completed by persons working for the RAD public utility company and members of the civilian protection. That evening, one or two trucks carrying dead bodies arrived, but it was on the following days that the trucks started to arrive in large numbers. In addition to the bodies that were collected from Kravica, they buried bodies that were collected from near the Konjevic Polje cross-road and from around the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac. The witness himself saw some of the dead bodies that lay near the Konjevic Polje intersection and in front of the Vuk Karadzic school. The witness estimated that around 400 to 500 bodies were buried over the three days that he attended at the Glogova grave-site. He does, however, believe that more bodies were buried at the location after he left the area. Mr. President, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you previously testified that you met with deputy commander of the Special Police Brigade Ljubisa Borovcanin at the Jasen restaurant in Bratunac and that that was the day you witnessed killings in Kravica. Aside from Mr. Borovcanin, who else was present at the Jasen restaurant with you?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: At the Jasen restaurant apart from Mr. Borovcanin and me, there were Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, Mr. Srbislav Davidovic, I think there was Mr. Ljubo Simic. Later we were joined by the police officer who was at the medical centre in Bratunac to be treated, and I think there were other people, actually I'm sure that there were other people present but I don't remember who.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether someone by the name of Dragan Josipovic, whose first name is Miodrag, was present?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And approximately what time did this gathering take place?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: It may have been around 7.00, 7.30, and we stayed maybe until 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: On whose initiative did you all meet?

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Ljubisa Borovcanin and I met somewhere in town. I invited Ljubisa to dinner to the Jasen restaurant and later on I met Srbislav Davidovic, Miroslav Deronjic, Ljubisa -- and I don't know who else and I said that I would have dinner at the Jasen with Ljubisa Borovcanin, so I told them to join us there so we could talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You just told us and you previously testified about a man who joined you who had been treated at the medical centre in Bratunac. Please tell us what you were told during your dinner about what had happened to that man.

utterances.speaker: PW-064
utterances.text: Before this young man arrived at the restaurant, I think Ljubisa Borovcanin said that he had a policeman from a special unit -- that one of the policeman were the special unit was killed and another was wounded. The incident occurred at Sandici or Kravica. One Muslim grabbed a rifle from a policeman and shot him. He killed him. The other policeman was nearby so he grabbed the barrel in order to avoid more casualties. They wrestled for the rifle and the barrel was probably or, rather, obviously very hot from the firing. That's why this lad burned his left hand or more precisely the fingers on his left hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May we have P1042 displayed, and specifically page 2 in the English version which corresponds to page 30 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you the log-book, which you have seen before, that shows the admission of patients to the Bratunac health centre in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if I could request the assistance of the Court Usher to hand the witness the original log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please do that. Did the Defence have the opportunity to look into this log-book?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Not at the original log-book, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's given to Mr. Gajic. The witness is now in the possession of this log-book. Ms. Hasan, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
